title: How Did Ancient Humans Keep Food Without a Fridge?

shots.text: Tonight, your fridge will hum in the dark.
Milk. Eggs. Leftovers. Safe for days.
Now rewind fifty thousand years.
A hunter brings down an antelope.
Far more meat than his family can eat.
And in this heat, it will rot within days.
No fridge. No ice.
So what does he do?
Trick one: the sun and the wind.
Thin strips, hung up to dry, keep for weeks.
Trick two: smoke.
It dries the meat, and keeps the flies away.
Trick three, up north: bury it in frozen ground.
Nature's own freezer.
But the smartest fridge wasn't a place at all.
shots.say: But the [smartest](/smˈɑɹtəst/) fridge wasn't a place at all.

shots.text: It was other people.
He shares the meat with the whole camp.
Next week, someone else gets lucky, and shares with him.
Researchers living with the Hadza of Tanzania still see this today.
shots.say: Researchers living with the [Hadza](/hˈɑdzə/) of Tanzania still see this today.

shots.text: Meat spoils. A favour doesn't.
Your fridge stores food.
Theirs stored friendship.
